in_context.text: Paul has just said that elders who lead well deserve double honour and fair pay (5:17-18). He now tells Timothy not to take up a charge against an elder unless two or three witnesses back it. The next verses say that those who do sin are to be rebuked publicly, with no favouritism (5:20-21).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer of the letter.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Elders in the church, the leaders Paul has just described as ruling and teaching (5:17), and anyone who might bring charges against them.

what.text: A rule of fair process. A formal accusation against an elder should not even be admitted on one person's word, only when two or three witnesses support it. This echoes the Old Testament law that one witness is not enough to establish a charge.

events.text: The instruction applies to the church at Ephesus while Timothy was leading it, after Paul had gone on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, by Paul, between his Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and think a follower wrote it in Paul's name; others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

where.text: Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Paul may have written from Macedonia, but the letter does not say.

purpose.text: Requiring two or three witnesses guards elders against an accusation that rests on one person's word. Verse 20 makes sure real sin is still dealt with openly.

big_picture.text: The rule applies a principle found across Scripture: matters are established by two or three witnesses. Moses' law, Jesus' teaching on church discipline, and Paul's own words to Corinth all use it.

for_readers.text: Churches should treat charges against leaders with fairness and care. They should neither believe every rumour nor shield a leader from real wrongdoing, and they must act 'without preferring one before another' (5:21).

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted to dismiss or silence complaints against pastors or church leaders, as if a leader cannot be questioned unless several people saw the wrong directly.

in_context_reading.text: The verse guards against unsupported charges, but the very next verses say that those who sin are to be rebuked 'before all.' Timothy is charged to act 'without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality' (5:20-21). The aim is fair judgment, not protection of leaders from accountability.

why_it_matters.text: The word can mean an older man, as in 5:1, or a church leader, as in 5:17. Coming right after 5:17-18, it most naturally points to the elders who rule and teach.
The word means to receive or admit. Timothy is told not even to admit a charge for consideration without witnesses, which is a step before any judgment.
The word means an accusation or charge. Titus 1:6 uses it of children "accused of riot."
The word is used here in a legal sense, as in Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1. It ties the verse to the biblical standard of evidence.

takeaway.text: Do not condemn a church leader on one person's unsupported word. When wrongdoing is confirmed, deal with it openly and without favouritism.

resolved.reason: The cited sources never say leaders are visible or easy targets for gossip or false charges. Verse 5:13 describes idle younger widows who tattle, not attacks on elders, so the stated rationale is the card's own reading rather than anything in the text.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources

resolved.reason: The lexicon lists John 18:29 as a use of the word, but neither it nor any cited source gives that verse's text or says the charge there was against Jesus.
